why: Briefing states flatly that no harness delivers a notification off the machine (no phone, no push); the user would have to build a forwarder themselves, which a normal user will not do. Impact is high because it converts the walk-away from a gamble into a real option and stops blocked sessions idling for the length of an errand.

Briefing: no harness distinguishes a wedged agent from a productive one, both keep emitting, and no harness estimates turn length. Telling them apart by hand means watching one pane over minutes and comparing against a mental baseline, which is correlation across time most people skip. Catching a thrashing agent early prevents concrete hours and token burn.

Requires recognizing a repeated pattern across many past sessions; briefing says no harness retains queryable history across sessions about what the user did or how often they were interrupted, so this is effectively unobtainable by hand. Impact is real but occasional: authoring a skill is a one-off improvement, not a recurring decision.

A session own subagents are visible in its own terminal (briefing cross-cutting fact one), so for the pane in front of you this is cheap; across 3-12 sessions it needs pane-cycling, and the tripwire half needs sustained watching that no harness supports. Briefing does not cover workflow-stage tripwires specifically, so I assumed the Spacedock stage strip is Cargento-only. Changes steering decisions regularly but rarely prevents outright loss.

Briefing: no harness retains queryable history across sessions, so streaks and weekly counts would mean parsing session files on disk over time. But the item own outcome is stated as no decision attached, and nothing follows from knowing it, so impact is near the floor regardless of how hard it is to get.

On Claude Code this is one command away (/usage reports quota) and a user running Barista sees cached weekly percentages and reset times unprompted, per the briefing. I scored the cross-harness case assuming the Claude split dominates since it is where the weekly window matters; on Codex only a current usage line exists and on most others quota is absent. Planning a week around a reset changes real decisions but at weekly, not hourly, cadence.

Briefing says Claude lifecycle hooks (Notification, SessionEnd) exist but a normal user has not wired them up, and no other harness is documented as offering this; a state-change notifier is a script the user could write but would not. Removes the recurring polling loop, which is a standing tax rather than a one-time win.

git status is explicitly listed as available to a resourceful user, so per repo it is one command; the hard part is knowing which sessions ended and where, which the briefing says no harness records (no cross-session view, no retained history). Scored as the several-places case. Impact is high because the loss is concrete uncommitted work.

This needs two things the briefing says are absent: no harness estimates how long the current turn will take, and no harness shows anything about other sessions. So a forward-looking all-clear across 3-12 panes is not obtainable by hand at all. Impact is a real repeated decision (leave the desk or not) short of preventing loss outright.

Briefing: quota where shown is a current figure only, and no harness projects a burn rate forward or attributes consumption to a session. A user could sample /usage twice and do the arithmetic, so it is not literally unobtainable, but doing it reliably enough to trust means correlating readings across time. Prevents a blown quota window mid-job.
